name: Aisha Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for making the time, Aisha. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and this is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you begin by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the train loadout at the phosphate mine. The rock comes off the stockpile by conveyor into a big silo, and when the train creeps underneath, I open the chute and fill each wagon to the right weight, one after another, about a hundred wagons a train. Get it wrong and a wagon goes over weight and the whole train waits. I've been doing it two and a half years. Before that I ran my parents' corner shop until the supermarket opened on the bypass and finished us.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's exact. There's a number on the screen and you either hit it or you don't. Hard is the night trains, and being junior so I get every Christmas shift. My husband Erik builds farm fences, his own little business, and it's good in spring and dead in winter, so my wage is the steady one and there's no fat on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, the sky didn't fall. I use the AI on my phone now and then for the church newsletter, so I'd say it's a handy helper and that's all. I'm not one to post my opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means life goes on, and I'm glad. The loadout already has a computer doing half the work, I just watch it and step in. If nothing big changes, I keep doing that and try to move up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, ask about the training to run the stacker as well so I'm more useful, and try to save a bit over winter when Erik's work is slow. Maybe I'd use the AI to help Erik write his quotes, he spends hours on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, really, it's one less thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the corner shop. Does that colour how you see this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. Nobody saw the supermarket as a threat until the car park was poured. So even when things seem calm, I keep half an eye out. But in this picture, there's nothing to see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about winters at home.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From June to August, Erik maybe gets two jobs a month. We live on my pay, we eat a lot of soup, and the kids know not to ask for much. It's fine, it's how we were both raised.

S0.say: She'd say the sky didn't fall and describe AI as a handy helper she uses now and then for the church newsletter. She doesn't post opinions online.
S0.think: She thinks life goes on as normal. The loadout already partly runs on a computer she supervises, and she'd keep doing that and try to move up.
S0.do: Keeps working and asks for training on the stacker to be more useful. Saves a little over winter and uses AI to help Erik write his fencing quotes.
S0.feel: Calm and happy that it's one less worry.
S0.quote: Nobody saw the supermarket as a threat until the car park was poured.
S0.fieldNote: Aisha is precise and practical, shaped by losing her family's shop. She already works alongside automation at the loadout without concern. Her household depends on her steady wage because her husband's business is seasonal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have to move with the times, that's how it works, my parents' shop learned that. But I'd also say a good employer trains its people instead of tossing them out. I'd say it at work and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the loadout goes fully automatic, it's halfway there already. They'd want one person in a control room watching three loadouts, not one at each. I'm junior, so I might not be the one in the chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be trained on the control room software as soon as one of the senior operators had done it and liked it. I'd get better at the AI tools, maybe with Johan's help, he's fourteen and quicker than me. And I'd start helping Erik on weekends, so if the mine goes, I already know the fencing trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but I'd be watching the noticeboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Helping Erik with fencing. Is that a real fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not glamorous, but people will always need fences, at least for a while. I can drive a post driver, I've done it on holidays. Two of us could take bigger jobs, and the money would stay in the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said businesses have to move with the times. Would you feel the same if it was your job going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel it, of course. But I don't think it's fair to ask a company to keep a job a machine does better. I'd just want them to be decent about how they do it.

S1.say: She'd say businesses must move with the times, as her parents' shop learned, but a good employer trains its people rather than discarding them.
S1.think: She thinks the loadout will go fully automatic and one control room will watch several loadouts. As a junior, she might not get the chair.
S1.do: Signs up for control room training once a senior operator has done it and approves. Improves her AI skills with her son's help and starts helping Erik with fencing on weekends as a fallback.
S1.feel: Uneasy, watching the noticeboard but not losing sleep.
S1.quote: I don't think it's fair to ask a company to keep a job a machine does better.
S1.fieldNote: Aisha accepts the company's right to automate, consistent with her free-market views, while expecting decency in how it's done. She waits for a trusted colleague's approval before retraining. Her husband's fencing business is a ready fallback she takes seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone, and families will have to pull together. I'd still say people should look for work, not wait for the government. But I wouldn't blame the people who need help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd lose the loadout within a year, and even Erik's fences aren't safe if robots can do hands-on work. Farmers won't buy a robot fencer in two years, they're slow to spend. So I'd bet on the fences, but I'd be scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go into the fencing business with Erik straight away, before the mine lets me go, so we've got a head start. We'd cut back to the bone, sell the caravan, and ask my brother for a loan to buy a second post driver. And I'd ask the church to pray for us, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach would be in knots every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Johan and Sofia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we're a family business now, and they'd help on Saturdays. Johan would like that, he loves the tractor. Sofia's ten, she'd cry about the caravan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said farmers are slow to spend. What if you're wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd be in real trouble, and I'd go to my family and Erik's family. We'd get by on what we grow and what we can trade. People did it before.

S2.say: She'd say it's too fast for anyone and families will have to pull together. People should look for work rather than wait for government, but she wouldn't blame those who need help.
S2.think: She thinks she'd lose the loadout within a year. Even Erik's fencing isn't safe, but she'd bet on farmers being slow to buy robot fencers.
S2.do: Leaves the mine early to join Erik's fencing business full-time and sells the caravan. Borrows from her brother for a second post driver and leans on church and family.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with her stomach in knots every day.
S2.quote: Farmers won't buy a robot fencer in two years, they're slow to spend.
S2.fieldNote: Aisha acts quickly in this picture, moving into the family business rather than waiting to be let go. Her bet rests on farmers being slow to adopt robots, which she knows may be wrong. Family and church are her safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so people should get to work on it now. I'd tell the young ones to get apprenticeships. And I'd say the government should support trade training rather than just hand out cheques.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to build up the fencing on the side and save a bit from the mine. When the loadout goes, I'd move across without starting from nothing. I'd be forty-eight, which isn't old for fencing if you're careful with your back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the mine and work weekends with Erik, saving the fencing money. In the second year, I'd do a short course in farm business so I can run the books and quotes properly. I'd sign Johan up for a carpentry apprenticeship when he's sixteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it feels like a manageable kind of anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI in the fencing business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the paperwork, yes, once I'd seen it help Erik. It could do his quotes and invoices, and maybe tell us which farms need work. I wouldn't let it near the posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up for those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My Saturdays, mostly, and our holiday at the coast. Choir practice is on Thursday, so I'd keep that. I need one thing that's just for me.

S3.say: She'd call five years fair warning, urge young people into apprenticeships and say government should support trade training rather than hand out cheques.
S3.think: She thinks five years allows her to build up fencing on the side and save, so when the loadout goes she won't start from nothing. At forty-eight, fencing is still possible if she's careful.
S3.do: Stays at the mine while working weekends with Erik and saving the fencing income. Takes a short farm business course in year two, and signs her son up for a carpentry apprenticeship at sixteen.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a manageable way.
S3.quote: I wouldn't let it near the posts.
S3.fieldNote: The five-year warning lets Aisha build her fallback gradually instead of jumping. She'd use AI for paperwork once proven but keep it out of the hands-on work. She protects one thing for herself, her choir practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so it's up to each of us to get ready. Work hard, learn a trade, look after your family. That's what my parents would have said, and I'd say it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I think we'd be all right. The mine would probably keep me most of that time, Erik's business would be bigger, and the kids would be grown. By the end, maybe even fencing has robots, but by then we'd own the business and could buy one ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, save steadily, and help Erik grow the business over the years, maybe hire a young apprentice. Around year five I'd look at whether a robot post driver makes sense for us. I'd make sure Johan and Sofia both have a trade or a qualification before it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a robot yourselves. That's quite a shift from earlier.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, isn't it. But it's the shop all over again: if we'd had the money, we'd have opened our own little supermarket. The ones who own the machines do fine, the ones who don't get left. With ten years, maybe we can be on the right side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Sofia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She wants to be a teacher, like her aunt. I'd want her to have that, people will always want a real person teaching their kids. I'd pay for it if I have to wash dishes on the side.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty and it's up to each person to prepare: work hard, learn a trade and look after your family, as her parents would have said.
S4.think: She thinks they'd be all right over a decade, with the mine keeping her most of that time, Erik's business growing and the children grown. If fencing gets robots, they could own one.
S4.do: Keeps her job, saves steadily and helps Erik grow the business, maybe hiring an apprentice. Considers buying a robot post driver around year five and ensures both children have a trade or qualification.
S4.feel: Uneasy but steady; she'd sleep fine.
S4.quote: The ones who own the machines do fine, the ones who don't get left.
S4.fieldNote: Aisha's thinking shifts in the long picture from defending against machines to owning one, drawing on the lesson of her parents' shop. Her traditional values come through in self-reliance and family. The decade gives her confidence rather than calm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because we'd be betting everything on farmers being slow and we'd have no savings behind us. What would help is a low-interest loan for small family businesses, and support for apprenticeships so young people can learn real trades. Not a handout, a hand up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about the small businesses, like Erik's and my parents' shop. Everyone talks about the big companies and their workers. The little ones disappear quietly and nobody writes about them.

headlineQuote: The little ones disappear quietly and nobody writes about them.
portrait: Aisha Hansen is a 43-year-old train loadout operator at a large phosphate mine, two and a half years in after her parents' corner shop was closed by a supermarket. Her husband Erik runs a seasonal fencing business, so her wage is the steady one, with no savings to spare. She is traditional, church-going and practical, and uses AI now and then once she's seen it help. She is calm in the plateau, uneasy in gradual change and alarmed by the two-year AGI picture, when she'd leave early to join Erik's fencing business. With more time she builds that business on the side and even considers owning a robot herself.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because the family would be betting everything on farmers being slow to buy robots, with no savings behind them.
whatWouldHelp: Low-interest loans for small family businesses and support for apprenticeships: a hand up rather than a handout.
